stops.name: Zoppola, the castle of his birth
stops.campa: A boy is born in Friuli, in the flat country between the Tagliamento and the Livenza, in a year the chroniclers will later disagree on: some say Portogruaro, some Udine, some this castle of Zoppola. His father's people come out of Delminium, an old Dalmatian town across the Adriatic, and the boy will take that town's name for his own: Camillo Delminio. Nothing marks the birth as extraordinary yet. But the region itself is a crossing-place, march of empires, and the boy who is born here will spend his life building a theatre meant to be the crossing-place of everything that has ever been said.

stops.name: Padua, the University, philosophy and jurisprudence
stops.campa: At Padua, seat of the most famous Aristotelian school in Italy, Camillo studies philosophy and jurisprudence among the sons of half of Europe's nobility. He is quick, ambitious, and already in love with rhetoric more than with law. Scholars will later wonder whether the young Camillo crossed paths here or later in Bologna with the astronomer Copernicus, who studies at Padua in these same years; no record proves it, but the two disciplines, the ordering of the heavens and the ordering of memory, will both obsess him for the rest of his life.

stops.name: San Vito al Tagliamento, teacher of eloquence and logic
stops.campa: Back in his own country, Camillo takes a post teaching eloquence and logic at the academy of San Vito al Tagliamento, seat of the lords who will soon give their name, Liviana, to a grander academy at Pordenone. He is a schoolmaster among the market towns of Friuli, drilling boys in Cicero's periods and Aristotle's figures, but he already speaks of memory as something more than a trick for orators: a ladder, if rightly built, by which the mind might climb to see everything at once, the way God sees it.

stops.name: Pordenone, the Accademia Liviana
stops.campa: In 1508 Camillo joins the short-lived Accademia Liviana at Pordenone, gathered under the patronage of the Lords of San Vito, called Liviani. Here he sits among poets and physicians of real standing: Girolamo Fracastoro, who will one day name syphilis and write of contagion in verse; Giovanni Cotta and Andrea Navagero, Venetian humanists of the first rank. It is a small academy and it will not outlast a generation, but it teaches Camillo that a room of the right minds, arranged in the right order, is itself a kind of memory theatre before he has built one of wood.

stops.name: Venice, lodging by the house of Aldus Manutius
stops.campa: Camillo takes lodging in the Sestiere di San Polo, hard by the house of Aldus Manutius, whose press has already put Aristotle and Aldus's italic Virgil into the hands of half of literate Europe. The printing quarter hums with proof-sheets and Greek type. To live here is to live at the address of the New Learning itself. Camillo, still a provincial schoolmaster by trade, begins to be known among the men who correct Aldus's texts and argue in his courtyard: the beginning of a Venetian fame that will, within twenty years, reach as far as the court of France.

stops.name: Venice, the friendship of Erasmus of Rotterdam
stops.campa: Among the Venetians whom Camillo comes to know is a visiting Dutchman correcting proofs for Aldus: Desiderius Erasmus. The two men are on easy terms in these Venetian years, close enough that Erasmus will later still call him an old acquaintance. It is a friendship the years will test hard: twenty years on, when Camillo's wooden Theatre is the talk of two kingdoms, this same Erasmus will judge it a dangerous folly. But in Venice, in the printing-house years, Camillo is simply one more clever young Italian in a city full of them.

stops.name: Venice, the circle of Titian, Aretino, Bembo, and Serlio
stops.campa: Camillo's Venice widens: he comes to know the painter Titian, already the most sought brush in the lagoon; Pietro Bembo, arbiter of the Italian tongue; the sharp-penned Pietro Aretino, whom he will correspond with for the rest of his life; and Sebastiano Serlio, the architect, whose treatises on the ancient theatre Camillo will one day plunder for his own reversed design. He is not yet the famous Camillo. He is a bright provincial finding his level among men who will, within a generation, be called the great age of Venetian art and letters.

stops.name: Rome, before Cardinal Egidio da Viterbo
stops.campa: Camillo travels to Rome and comes into the orbit of Cardinal Egidio da Viterbo, the great Augustinian prior whose Scechina is the master text of Christian Kabbalah in Italy, and whose circle includes the Venetian friar Francesco Giorgi. From this meeting, scholars will trace the current that runs into Camillo's Theatre: the Sephirot, the three worlds, the angels ranked over the planets, all drawn from the Kabbalah that Pico della Mirandola had baptized into Christian philosophy a generation before. Camillo leaves Rome carrying, half-formed, the scaffolding on which his whole Theatre will one day be raised.

stops.name: Venice, the first stirring of the Theatre
stops.campa: Back in Venice, Camillo begins in earnest the labor that will occupy him for the next twenty-five years: the Idea of the Theatre. Johann Sturm will later call it the fruit of forty years' work, counting back from Camillo's death almost exactly to this year. He does not yet call it a building. He calls it, in the treatise he is drafting, a workshop where every human thought might be given its own fixed place, to be found again at will, the whole of learning laid out at a glance the way a merchant lays out his goods on a table.
stops.quote: The reason is from knowing that in the great workshop of 'Teatro' are disposed through loci and images all the places necessary to locate and minister to all human concepts, everything in the entire world, not only those pertaining to all sciences and the noble and mechanic arts.
stops.quote_source: Trattato dell'Imitatione (Treatise on Imitation), trans. Kate Robinson

stops.name: Bologna, the chair of Dialectics
stops.campa: Camillo is given, for some years, a chair of Dialectics at the University of Bologna, oldest of the schools of Europe. He lectures on logic to law students and future physicians, and he is remembered, even by his rivals, as a teacher who could turn dry syllogism into something like poetry. It is here, Torquato Tasso will later say, that Camillo shows for the first time since Dante that rhetoric itself is a kind of poetry: not ornament laid over thought, but thought's own natural shape.

stops.name: Bologna, the fame of the great inventor
stops.campa: Word of Camillo's method spreads beyond the lecture hall. Ariosto, finishing his Orlando Furioso, will place him among the noblemen of the final canto as one who leads readers 'by a shorter pathway to the Ascraean font divine,' the fountain of Hesiod himself. Liruti, writing two centuries later, will simply call him 'Giulio Camillo, great inventor of ways to make the sciences easy.' None of this fame yet has a building attached to it. It is the fame of a man everyone agrees is extraordinary and no one has quite seen prove it.

stops.name: Venice, the reversal: the spectator upon the stage
stops.campa: The design comes clear to Camillo: he will not build a memory-room for a single orator to walk through, as the ancients taught, but a theatre proper, on the model Vitruvius gives for Rome, with its seven gangways and rising seats. Then he inverts it entire. In his Theatre no audience sits watching a play; a single spectator stands where the stage would be, and looks outward and upward at the whole cosmos, ranked in the seats before him, legible at a glance from that one point. Scholar and orator alike is to become spectator of everything at once.
stops.quote: Now if the ancient orators, wishing to place from day to day the parts of the speeches which they had to recite, confided them to frail places as frail things, it is right that we, wishing to store up eternally the eternal nature of all things which can be expressed in speech, should assign them to eternal places. Our high labour, therefore, has been to find an order in these seven measures, capacious and distinct from one another, and which will keep the mind awake and move the memory.
stops.quote_source: L'Idea del Theatro (Florence, 1550), trans. Frances Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
